why: The instrument, before the measurements. PIZERO-98 cannot start without it, and every later performance claim needs a baseline to compare against. Cheap: the telemetry already exists, nothing captures it.
The headline number for goals 1-4: hours of continuous 60 Hz, dropouts and freezes per hour. Closes PIZERO-33 either way, with a clean run or with the root-cause evidence it was built to catch.
The worst daily-use defect: a device pulled out is invisible, so nothing works until reboot. Also the leading freeze suspect, so it is on the critical path for goal 4, not just for USB comfort.
Runs on the laptop in seconds and protects the audio and HDMI packet logic behind goals 2 and 3. PIZERO-100 is a four-line test we never had. Forces extraction from main.cpp, which is the point.

The first-run experience for anyone handed a kit: a missing ROM currently shows a black screen with no explanation. Small, self-contained, and it is what makes the kit survivable without you on the phone.

Goal 3 on other people's screens. The 60 Hz timing has narrowed porches and has only ever been proven on one lenient monitor. Gates the kit batch; a sink that refuses it is a bug we want now, not after shipping.

The case is critical for the first edition and this is the last known defect in it: the card is flush and hard to grip. Batched with PIZERO-104 and PIZERO-105 into one print, which should close three tickets at once.

How much frame time is actually left at 60 Hz, USB and keyboard included. Everything after this is arithmetic against this number: CoCo 3 modes, the overlay, hub support. The current figure predates both audio and 60 Hz.
Turns vetting from a one-off event into something every build repeats. Depends on PIZERO-108 for the record format, so it follows rather than leads.
Goal 2 is continuous sound; this is sound that is also correct. Pitch and tone against desktop XRoar, with the ACR question in PIZERO-32 riding along.
Answers whether CoCo 3 is a programme or an aspiration, in numbers rather than instinct. Needs PIZERO-88 first, which is why it sits here: a cheap analysis that prevents an expensive misjudgement.

Overlay programme starts here, once vetting is done. The catalogue is the only slice with no rendering or timing risk, and it is verifiable over serial before anything is drawn. Wider than Fruit Jam: DSK, BIN and CART.

The look: a VDG-format card blitted through the machine's own path, so the overlay reads as part of the CoCo rather than a menu over it. Carries the one real design risk, double buffering, which Fruit Jam never had to solve.

The feel: F12, key capture that cannot leak into BASIC, paging, and a pause that keeps HDMI audio streaming. Responsiveness is an acceptance criterion here, not a polish item, and the audio constraint is cheap now and painful later.

Decide before building the launch path, not after: cold boot, hot swap, or both on different keys. Fruit Jam is inconsistent with itself here, which is the evidence that leaving it implicit does not work.
Selecting something finally starts it. Blocked on porting coco_machine_reset() from the AMOLED port, and on the PIZERO-115 decision, which is why it is last of the four slices.
